name: Subclavian artery
func: The main artery to each arm. It arches over the top of the lung beneath the collarbone and also gives branches to the brain (vertebral artery), neck, shoulder and front chest wall.

levels.kid:
Your arms need blood too! The **subclavian artery** is the big blood tube that carries it there.

"Sub" means under and "clavian" means collarbone, so its name says where it is: just under your collarbone. You have one on each side.

It comes out from near your heart, makes an arch over the very top of your lung, and then slips out toward your armpit. After that, it gets a new name and keeps going down your arm.

On the way it gives off some branches, including a little one that climbs up your neck to help feed the back of your brain.
levels.hs:
The two subclavian arteries start differently: the **right subclavian** comes from the **brachiocephalic trunk** behind the right sternoclavicular joint, while the **left subclavian** comes straight off the **aortic arch**. Each arches over the top of the lung (the **cervical pleura**) and passes behind the clavicle.

A muscle in the side of the neck, **scalenus anterior**, crosses in front of it and divides it into three parts: the first part (before the muscle), the second part (behind it) and the third part (after it). The artery passes through the gap between the **anterior and middle scalene** muscles together with the roots of the **brachial plexus**, the nerve network for the arm. The **subclavian vein** passes in front of scalenus anterior, separated from the artery.

At the outer border of the **first rib**, the subclavian artery changes its name to the **axillary artery**.

Main branches (mostly from the first part) include the **vertebral artery** (to the brain), the **internal thoracic artery** (down the inside of the front chest wall), the **thyrocervical trunk** (to the thyroid, neck and shoulder) and the **costocervical trunk** (to the neck muscles and upper ribs).
levels.college:
Branches by part (a common mnemonic is "**VIT C, D**"): the first part gives the **Vertebral**, **Internal thoracic** and **Thyrocervical trunk**; the second part gives the **Costocervical trunk**; the third part often gives the **Dorsal scapular artery** (which may instead come from the transverse cervical). On the left, the costocervical trunk usually arises from the first part.

The **thyrocervical trunk** gives the **inferior thyroid**, **suprascapular** and **transverse cervical** arteries; the inferior thyroid artery is closely related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, a key point in thyroid surgery.

The **internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery** runs down about 1 cm from the sternal edge behind the costal cartilages, giving anterior intercostal branches, and ends by dividing into the **musculophrenic** and **superior epigastric** arteries. Surgeons prize it as the best conduit for **coronary bypass**, with long-term patency far exceeding vein grafts.

Relations: the **right recurrent laryngeal nerve** loops under the right subclavian; the **phrenic nerve** descends on the front of scalenus anterior; the **vagus** crosses the first part; and the **thoracic duct** arches over the left subclavian to empty near the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins.

Its pulse can be compressed against the first rib behind the middle of the clavicle to control bleeding from the arm.
levels.phd:
The two subclavians have different embryological origins, which is why they look asymmetrical. The **right subclavian** derives from the right **fourth pharyngeal arch artery** proximally and the right **seventh intersegmental artery** distally; the **left subclavian** comes entirely from the left seventh intersegmental artery, which migrates upward as the aortic arch remodels.

If the right fourth arch artery regresses abnormally, the right subclavian instead arises as the **last branch of the aortic arch** and crosses behind the esophagus: an **aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria)**, in about 0.5–2% of people. It's usually silent but can cause difficulty swallowing (**dysphagia lusoria**). Because the right recurrent laryngeal nerve normally hooks under the right fourth-arch-derived subclavian, an aberrant artery leaves a **non-recurrent laryngeal nerve** that runs directly to the larynx, a hazard in thyroid surgery.

Hemodynamically, a proximal subclavian stenosis lowers pressure in the arm and the vertebral artery's origin, reversing the pressure gradient so blood flows **retrograde down the vertebral artery** (subclavian steal). Most people with this flow reversal on ultrasound have no symptoms, because the circle of Willis and other collaterals compensate, an illustration of how robust the brain's redundant supply is.

The artery's course through the scalene triangle and over the first rib makes it susceptible to repetitive compression and post-stenotic dilation, which can generate thrombus and emboli to the hand.
levels.expert:
**Subclavian stenosis** (usually atherosclerosis, more often on the left) causes a **blood pressure difference of more than about 15 mmHg between the arms**, a weaker pulse on one side, arm fatigue with use and sometimes a supraclavicular bruit. **Subclavian steal syndrome** adds vertebrobasilar symptoms (dizziness, visual disturbance, imbalance) when the arm is exercised. Always measure blood pressure in both arms; the higher one is the true reading.

**Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS)** compresses the neurovascular bundle at the scalene triangle, costoclavicular space or under pectoralis minor. A **cervical rib** is a classic cause. **Neurogenic TOS** (brachial plexus, most common) gives pain and tingling down the inner arm and hand-muscle wasting; **arterial TOS** (rare but serious) causes aneurysm, emboli and a cold, pale hand; **venous TOS** causes arm swelling and vein thrombosis, often after repetitive overhead activity.

Trauma: clavicle fractures, penetrating injuries and line placement can injure the artery. During **subclavian central line** insertion, accidental arterial puncture is hard to compress because the clavicle is in the way, and the lung apex lies just below, so **pneumothorax** is a known complication.

A **Pancoast tumor** at the lung apex can invade the subclavian vessels, the lower brachial plexus and the sympathetic chain (Horner syndrome).

Imaging: duplex ultrasound, CT or MR angiography. Treatment in general terms: risk-factor control and antiplatelets, **angioplasty and stenting** or surgical bypass for symptomatic disease, and surgical decompression (sometimes removing a cervical or first rib) for TOS.

keyPoints: Right arises from brachiocephalic trunk; left from the aortic arch
Divided into 3 parts by scalenus anterior
Becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the 1st rib
Branches: vertebral, internal thoracic, thyrocervical, costocervical, dorsal scapular
Arm BP difference >15 mmHg suggests stenosis; subclavian steal reverses vertebral flow
Thoracic outlet syndrome compresses it with the brachial plexus

test.q: The left subclavian artery arises from the:
test.explain: The right comes from the brachiocephalic trunk; the left comes directly off the arch.

test.q: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the first ______.
test.explain: Same vessel, new name, as it passes into the axilla.

test.q: Which muscle divides the subclavian artery into three parts?
test.explain: Scalenus anterior crosses in front of the artery; the vein passes in front of the muscle.

test.q: In subclavian steal, blood flows backward down the:
choices: Vertebral artery on the same side
test.explain: Proximal stenosis drops pressure so the vertebral feeds the arm instead of the brain.

test.q: Which subclavian branch is the preferred conduit for coronary bypass surgery?
test.explain: The internal thoracic artery has excellent long-term patency as a bypass graft.
